segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: How are you getting on with your art project, Tom?

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: OK. Like, they gave us the theme of birds to base our project on, and I’m not really all that interested in wildlife. But I’m starting to get into it. I’ve pretty well finished the introductory stage.

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: So have I. When they gave us all those handouts with details of books and websites to look at , I was really put off, but the more I read, the more interested I got.

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: Me too. I found I could research so many different aspects of birds in art – colour, movement, texture. So I was looking forward to the Bird Park visit.

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: What a letdown! It poured with rain and we hardly saw a single bird. Much less use than the trip to the Natural History Museum .

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: Yeah, I liked all the stuff about evolution there. The workshop sessions with Dr Fletcher were good too, especially the brainstorming sessions.

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: I missed those because I was ill. I wish we could’ve seen the projects last year’s students did.

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: Mm. I suppose they want us to do our own thing, not copy.

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: Have you drafted your proposal yet?

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: Yes, but I haven’t handed it in. I need to amend some parts. I’ve realised the notes from my research are almost all just descriptions, I haven’t actually evaluated anything. So I’ll have to fix that .

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: Oh, I didn’t know we had to do that. I’ll have to look at that too. Did you do a timeline for the project?

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: Yes, and a mind map.

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: Yeah, so did I. I quite enjoyed that. But it was hard having to explain the basis for my decisions in my action plan.

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: What?

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: You know, give a rationale.

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: I didn’t realise we had to do that. OK, I can add it now. And I’ve done the video diary presentation, and worked out what I want my outcome to be in the project.

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: Someone told me it’s best not to be too precise about your actual outcome at this stage, so you have more scope to explore your ideas later on. So I’m going to do back to my proposal to make it a bit more vague.

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: Really? OK, I’ll change that too then.

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: One part of the project, I’m unsure about is where we choose some paintings of birds and say what they mean to us. Like, I chose a painting of a falcon by Landseer. I like it because the bird’s standing there with his head turned to one side, but he seems to be staring straight at you. But I can’t just say it’s a bit scary, can I?

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: You could talk about the possible danger suggested by the bird’s look.

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: There’s a picture of a fish hawk by Audubon I like. It’s swooping over the water with a fish in its talons, and with great black wings which take up most of the picture.

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: So you could discuss it in relation to predators and food chains?

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: Well actually I think I’ll concentrate on the impression of rapid motion it gives.

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: Right.

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: Do you know that picture of a kingfisher by van Gosh – it’s perching on a reed growing near a stream.

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: Yes, it’s got these beautiful blue and red and black shades.

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: Mm hm. I’ve actually chosen it because I saw a real kingfisher once when I was litter, I was out walking with my grandfather, and I’ve never forgotten it.

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: So we can use a personal link?

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: Sure.

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: OK. There’s a portrait called William Wells. I can’t remember the artist but it’s a middle-aged man who’s just shot a bird. And his expression, and the way he’s holding the bird in his hand suggests he’s not sure about what he’s done. To me it’s about how ambiguous people are in the way they exploit the natural world.

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: Interesting. There’s Gauguin’s picture Vairumati. He did it in Tahiti. It’s a woman with a white bird behind her that is eating a lizard, and what I’m interested in is what idea this bird refers to. Apparently, it’s a reference to the never-ending cycle of existence.

segments.speaker: TOM
segments.en: Wow. I chose a portrait of a little boy, Giovanni de Medici. He’s holding a tiny bird in one fist. I like the way he’s holding it carefully so he doesn’t hurt it.

segments.speaker: JESS
segments.en: Ah right.
